848.title: The beginning of knowledge (Proverbs 1:7)
848.hook: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge"
848.carry: the first step through the door
848.howItsDone: Mishlei is part of the Writings. Jews study it as practical wisdom for daily life, and its sayings are quoted at tables, in classrooms and in synagogue teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the book of Job ended with a surprise: the friends with tidy answers were wrong, and the man who cried out was right. Did you manage one kind thought toward someone who hurt you? Today, a new book, and a very different voice. Day eight hundred forty-eight.

A grandmother's saying. A line taped above a desk. Something a coach shouted once that a player still repeats years later. Short sayings travel. They fit in a pocket, and they come out at the right moment, often when the long explanation has been forgotten. After Job, with its long speeches and its storm, the Writings turn to a whole book of these pocket sentences. One or two lines each. Easy to say, hard to live. Today's word is that book's Hebrew name.
screen: `A GRANDMOTHER'S SAYING.` → `SHORT SAYINGS TRAVEL.` → `A WHOLE BOOK OF THEM.`

segments.voice: Mishlei. It's the Hebrew name of the book English calls Proverbs, taken from its opening words: the proverbs of Solomon the son of David, king of Israel. Tradition links the book to Solomon, the king remembered for asking God for wisdom. The book itself also names other voices further on, so it reads less like one lecture and more like a family's collected advice. The opening verses say why the book exists: to know wisdom, to understand words of insight, so that the simple can grow shrewd and the young can gain knowledge. And then, before any advice is given, comes the line the whole book stands on: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge." Fear here is a word worth sitting with. Some readers hear awe, the feeling of standing before something far bigger than yourself. Others hear a plainer fear: the care not to do wrong in God's sight, a respect that changes how a person acts. Jewish teachers have read it more than one way, and both readings are in the conversation. Notice the word beginning. Not the end of knowledge, as if faith replaces thinking. The beginning. Awe is where learning starts, the first step through the door, not a wall at the end of the hall. There's a picture in that. Job ended with God showing him stars and sea, and Job going quiet. Mishlei starts from that same quiet, and builds a daily life on it: how to speak, how to work, how to treat a neighbor. Proverbs are small, but they assume something large behind them. The beginning of knowledge.
screen: `MISHLEI: THE PROVERBS OF SOLOMON.` · `WHY THE BOOK EXISTS.` · then, large: `THE FEAR OF THE LORD IS THE BEGINNING OF KNOWLEDGE.` · then: `AWE IS WHERE LEARNING STARTS.`

segments.voice: The practice today is to learn one proverb by heart. Take today's line: the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge. Or, if you'd rather, choose any single verse from the book of Proverbs you already know. Say it once, slowly. Then again, with your eyes closed. Then once more, letting each word land. While the bell rings, keep it turning, until you can say it without reaching for it. If you pray, you can let it be a prayer. If not, let it simply be yours. The bell holds the time.
Mishlei. The Hebrew name for the book of Proverbs, from its opening words, the proverbs of Solomon: short sayings for a whole life. Today's word.
Your line: the first step through the door. Today, before you try to figure something out, pause for one breath of awe at how much you don't know. Day eight hundred forty-eight.

849.title: A tree of life (Proverbs 3:17–18)
849.hook: sung as the Torah returns to the ark: "Her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace"
849.howItsDone: In synagogue services, as the Torah scroll is returned to the ark, congregations sing Etz chayim hi, the verses from Proverbs 3:18 and 3:17, before the ark is closed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mishlei opened with its foundation: the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge. Can you still say it without looking? Your line was the first step through the door. Today, two verses from the same book that left the page and became a song. Day eight hundred forty-nine.

The reading is over. The scroll has been lifted, rolled and dressed again in its cover. It's carried back toward the ark at the front of the synagogue, and the doors stand open. As it goes in, the congregation sings. The song's opening lines aren't new words written for the moment. They're two verses lifted straight out of the book of Proverbs. Wisdom and Torah, sung in one breath, and then the doors close on the scroll.
screen: `THE READING IS OVER.` → `THE SCROLL RETURNS TO THE ARK.` → `TWO VERSES FROM PROVERBS.`

segments.voice: Here are the verses, in the words of the King James text. "She is a tree of life to them that lay hold upon her." And just before it: "Her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace." In Proverbs, the she is wisdom. The chapter describes her like a person: more precious than rubies, with long life in one hand and riches and honor in the other. Wisdom is someone to walk beside. Then the synagogue does something quiet and bold. It sings those verses about the Torah. As the scroll goes back into the ark, wisdom and Torah are heard as one. The Torah becomes the tree, and the people singing are the ones holding on. Notice the verb: lay hold upon her. A tree of life isn't something you admire from a distance. You grab it. You hold on. The tradition gives this a physical shape too: the wooden rollers a Torah scroll is wound on are called atzei chayim, trees of life. Every time someone lifts the scroll, their hands are literally on the trees. And then the second verse. Her ways are ways of pleasantness. Some Jewish teachers have used this line as a test: in the Talmud, a reading of the law that would bring needless hardship is set aside, because her ways are pleasant. All her paths are peace. Peace here is shalom, a word with room in it for wholeness, for things being as they should be. So the song asks a lot of the people who sing it. Hold on to the tree. And choose the path that leads to peace.
screen: `WISDOM, LIKE A PERSON.` · `SUNG AS THE TORAH RETURNS.` · then, large: `SHE IS A TREE OF LIFE.` · then: `ALL HER PATHS ARE PEACE.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to take the pleasant path once. Let one choice from today come to mind: a message to answer, a chore, a conversation, a line at the store. Picture two ways through it. One sharper, one gentler. You don't have to decide now. Just see both clearly. Then let your hands close lightly, as if holding on to something steady. If you pray, you can say the line silently: all her paths are peace. If not, just breathe and hold the picture. The bell holds the time.
A tree of life. In Proverbs, wisdom; in the synagogue, the Torah; and the name of the wooden rollers people hold when they lift the scroll. Today's word.
Your line: all her paths are peace. Today, when you reach a fork, sharp or gentle, take the gentler path once, and notice what follows. Day eight hundred forty-nine.

850.title: A soft answer (Proverbs 15:1)
850.carry: a soft tongue breaketh the bone
850.howItsDone: Jewish teaching on careful speech draws on verses like Proverbs 15:1, and the line is quoted at home and in the classroom when an argument starts to rise.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two verses from Proverbs became the song sung as the Torah returns to the ark. She is a tree of life. Your line was all her paths are peace. Did you take the gentler path once? Today, Proverbs shows what that path sounds like. Day eight hundred fifty.

The text arrives at 9:40 at night. It's short, and it's sharp, and it ends with a period that somehow feels like a slammed door. A reply starts forming almost at once: accurate, cutting, impossible to argue with. Sending it would be satisfying for a minute or two. Then the phone buzzes again, and it's worse, and now two people are awake and angry. Proverbs has a sentence for the moment before you hit send. Today's line.
screen: `A SHARP TEXT AT NIGHT.` → `THE PERFECT REPLY.` → `THE MOMENT BEFORE SEND.`

segments.voice: Proverbs chapter fifteen, verse one, in the words of the King James text: "A soft answer turneth away wrath." And the second half finishes the thought: grievous words stir up anger. Two halves, side by side. One road and its opposite, and you can see where each one ends. The Hebrew for soft here is rakh. It's the word for something tender and gentle. It doesn't mean silent, and it doesn't mean giving in. A soft answer is still an answer. It still says something. It just says it in a way that lets the other person lower their guard. Later in the book, Proverbs pushes the idea further, with a picture that sounds almost impossible: a soft tongue breaketh the bone. Gentleness, it says, can do what force can't. The Tanakh has a story that shows it. In the book of Judges, after a battle, the men of Ephraim come to Gideon furious. Why didn't you call us to fight? They chide him sharply. Gideon could have fired back. Instead he answers by praising them: what have I done, compared with you? And the text says their anger toward him abated when he said that. A quarrel ends in one sentence. Notice what Proverbs is not saying. It doesn't promise that a soft answer always works, or that anger is never deserved. It simply sets the two roads side by side and lets you see where each one usually ends. Harsh words feed a fire. Soft ones give it nothing to burn. A soft answer.
screen: `TWO HALVES, TWO ROADS.` · then, large: `A SOFT ANSWER TURNETH AWAY WRATH.` · `RAKH: TENDER, NOT SILENT.` · then: `GIDEON AND THE MEN OF EPHRAIM.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to answer softly once. First, a rehearsal. Bring to mind a conversation that tends to get heated: a sibling, a coworker, someone at home. Hear the sharp thing they usually say. Now, instead of the cutting reply, find one soft sentence that is still true. Say it silently, and notice your shoulders as you do. Then breathe out slowly, and rest. If you pray, you can ask for a soft answer when it counts. The bell holds the time.
Rakh. Hebrew for soft: tender words that still say something, and turn anger away instead of feeding it. Today's word.
Your line: a soft tongue breaketh the bone. Today, when something sharp comes at you, wait one breath, and send back the softest true sentence you can find. Day eight hundred fifty.

851.title: His own way (Proverbs 22:6)
851.hook: train a child "in the way he should go"; commentators read it as each child's own way
851.howItsDone: Jewish teachers and parents quote Proverbs 22:6, reading 'according to his way' as a reason to teach each child in a way that fits that child.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Proverbs fifteen: a soft answer turneth away wrath, and Gideon cooled a quarrel with one sentence. Your line was a soft tongue breaketh the bone. Did a sharp moment get a softer reply? Today, a verse about raising children, and a small Hebrew word that changes it. Day eight hundred fifty-one.

Two kids, same house, same parents, same bedtime story read the same way. One wants to hear it again and again. The other has already wandered off to take the radio apart. The same lesson can land on one and slide right off the other. Proverbs has a famous verse about training children. Read quickly, it sounds like a rule for everyone. Read slowly, in Hebrew, it might be saying something else.
screen: `TWO KIDS, ONE HOUSE.` → `ONE LESSON, TWO RESULTS.` → `READ IT SLOWLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in the words of the King James text: "Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it." It sounds simple. Pick the right path, put the child on it, and hold them there until it sticks. But look at the Hebrew. The phrase translated in the way he should go is, word for word, closer to: according to his way. Al pi darko. His way. Whose way is that? Some commentators read it as the way a child ought to go, the path set out for everyone. Others notice that little his, and read it as the child's own way: his nature, his pace, the shape of his mind. Teach each child according to who that child is. The one who wants the story again and the one taking the radio apart may both learn, but not by the same road. There's another layer. The verb for train is chanokh. Elsewhere in the Tanakh the same verb is used for dedicating a new house. So training a child, on this reading, is less like pushing and more like a beginning: opening something, setting it on its way. And then the promise. When he is old, he will not depart from it. On the second reading, that promise has a reason inside it: a way that was the child's own from the start is a way the child can keep. The verse doesn't settle which reading is right, and Jewish teachers have held both. Either way, the little word his is still sitting there in the Hebrew. Each child's own way.
screen: `TRAIN UP A CHILD.` · then, large: `AL PI DARKO: ACCORDING TO HIS WAY.` · `CHANOKH: TO TRAIN, TO DEDICATE.` · then: `HE WILL NOT DEPART FROM IT.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to teach someone in their way. Bring to mind one person you sometimes teach or explain things to: a child, a student, a new coworker, a parent learning a phone. Picture them clearly. How do they actually learn? By doing, by asking, by watching, by hearing a story? Let one small change come to mind, one way you could meet them on their road instead of yours. Hold that picture while the bell rings. If you pray, you can pray for that person by name. The bell holds the time.
Darko. His way, the phrase from Proverbs that might mean the right road for all, or each child's own. Today's word.
Your line: each child's own way. Today, when you explain something to someone, try their road once: a story, a picture, a hands-on try. Day eight hundred fifty-one.

852.title: Give him bread (Proverbs 25:21)
852.hook: "If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat"
852.howItsDone: Jewish teaching links Proverbs 25:21 with the Torah's commands to help an enemy's stray or overloaded animal (Exodus 23:4–5), and the line is studied as part of how to treat people you're in conflict with.

segments.voice: Yesterday, train up a child according to his way, and the small Hebrew word that might mean each child's own way. Your line was each child's own way. Did you try someone else's road once? Today, Proverbs sets a place for a guest nobody invites. Day eight hundred fifty-two.

Someone knocks just as the bread comes out of the oven. Handing a slice to a friend would take no thought at all. Now change one thing. The person standing at the door, hungry, is someone you'd rather not see. The neighbor who complained about you. The coworker who took the credit. Someone who once wished you harm, and said so. Does the bread still get handed over? Proverbs answers that question in one plain sentence.
screen: `BREAD FRESH FROM THE OVEN.` → `CHANGE ONE THING.` → `WHO IS AT THE DOOR?`

segments.voice: Proverbs twenty-five, in the words of the King James text: "If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink." No other conditions. Not if he apologizes. Not if he's earned it. If he's hungry. The need comes first, and the history comes second. The verse goes on with a strange picture: for thou shalt heap coals of fire upon his head, and the LORD shall reward thee. Readers differ on the coals. Some hear the burning shame of being treated kindly by someone you wronged, a shame that might turn into regret. Others hear the coals as warmth, a kindness that melts the hostility. The verse doesn't explain itself, and it's fine to leave the picture open. This isn't a stray line. The Torah already says something close. In Exodus, if you find your enemy's ox or donkey wandering, you bring it back. If the donkey of someone who hates you is lying under its load, you help lift it. The rule doesn't ask you to like the person. It asks you to help with the animal. And there's a story. In the book of Kings, an army from Aram comes after the prophet Elisha, and is struck so it can't see where it's going. Elisha leads the soldiers into Samaria, into the hands of the king of Israel. The king asks, shall I strike them? Elisha says no: set bread and water before them, and send them home. So the king prepares a great meal. They eat, they drink, they go back to their master. And the text says the raiding bands of Aram came no more into the land of Israel. The very next verse brings a full war, so the peace is not forever. But the raids ended at a table, not at sword point. Give him bread.
screen: `THE NEED COMES FIRST.` · then, large: `IF THINE ENEMY BE HUNGRY, GIVE HIM BREAD.` · `HELP LIFT YOUR ENEMY'S DONKEY.` · then: `ELISHA SETS A TABLE.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to feed someone you dislike, or at least to get ready to. Bring one person to mind, someone you'd usually walk the long way around to avoid. Picture them a little hungry, a little tired, the way anyone gets. Now picture handing them something small: a coffee, a snack, a share of what's on the table. You don't have to feel warm about it. Just see your hand reaching out. If you pray, you can ask for an open hand. The bell holds the time.
Give him bread. Proverbs twenty-five, verse twenty-one: if your enemy is hungry, feed him. The need comes before the history. Today's word.
Your line: give him bread. Today, offer one small thing to eat or drink to someone who isn't your favorite person, and don't explain why. Day eight hundred fifty-two.

853.title: All is breath (Ecclesiastes 1:2)
853.hook: "vanity of vanities"; the Hebrew hevel means breath or vapor
853.howItsDone: Kohelet (Ecclesiastes) is one of the five scrolls of the Writings, and Ashkenazi communities read it in synagogue during the festival of Sukkot.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Proverbs said: if thine enemy be hungry, give him bread, and Elisha fed an army and sent it home. Your line was give him bread. Did someone unexpected get a share? Today, Proverbs gives way to a stranger, sadder, more searching book. Day eight hundred fifty-three.

Breathe on a cold window. A small cloud appears on the glass, clear and gray, and for a moment you could write your name in it. Then, while you watch, it shrinks from the edges and is gone. The glass looks exactly as it did before. One book of the Tanakh takes that little cloud and holds it up to everything: work, money, wisdom, pleasure, fame, a whole lifetime. Its opening cry is one word, said again and again. Today's word.
screen: `BREATH ON A COLD WINDOW.` → `GONE WHILE YOU WATCH.` → `ONE WORD, AGAIN AND AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Hevel. The book is Ecclesiastes, in Hebrew Kohelet, named for its speaker, the one the King James text calls the Preacher. And here is how he begins, in the King James words: "Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity." Every vanity in that line is the same Hebrew word: hevel. And hevel is not about pride or mirrors. Its plain picture is breath. Vapor. The mist that rises off a cup and isn't there a moment later. So the line can be heard another way: breath of breaths, all is breath. That changes the feeling of the book. Vanity sounds like a verdict: worthless. Breath is something else. Breath is real. You can feel it on your hand. It's what keeps you alive. It just can't be held. Kohelet looks at everything people chase, and says, again and again, hevel. You build, and someone else inherits. You grow wise, and the wise die like the foolish. You gather, and it slips away. There's an echo here, too. In Genesis, the brother who is killed, whom English calls Abel, is in Hebrew named Hevel. A life like a breath. Some readers find Kohelet bleak. Others find him honest, even freeing: if everything is breath, you can stop gripping. Either way, the word asks for a light touch. Not that nothing is real, but that nothing stays in the hand. All is breath.
screen: `KOHELET, THE PREACHER.` · then, large: `VANITY OF VANITIES: BREATH OF BREATHS.` · `REAL, BUT IMPOSSIBLE TO HOLD.` · then: `ABEL, IN HEBREW, IS HEVEL.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is simply to breathe out slowly. Sit comfortably. Breathe in through your nose, no strain. Then let the breath out, slowly, through your mouth, longer than the breath in. Feel it leave. Notice that you can't hold on to it, and that you don't need to: another comes. Keep that rhythm, letting each breath out be a little longer and softer. If a worry rises, let it ride out on the breath. If you pray, you can let one breath out carry a word of prayer. The bell holds the time.
Hevel. Breath, vapor, mist: the word the King James text renders as vanity, Kohelet's word for everything people try to hold. Today's word.

Your line: nothing stays in the hand. Today, when you catch yourself gripping something too tightly, a plan, an argument, a worry, let out one long breath and loosen your hand. Day eight hundred fifty-three.

854.title: A season (Ecclesiastes 3:1–8)
854.hook: "To every thing there is a season"
854.howItsDone: Ecclesiastes 3 belongs to Kohelet, one of the five scrolls of the Writings, and some Jews quote its 'a time to' lines at turning points in life, from celebrations to houses of mourning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kohelet's opening cry: hevel, breath of breaths. Your line was nothing stays in the hand. Did you loosen your grip on something? Today, the same book turns its breath into a rhythm, and the week comes to a close. Day eight hundred fifty-four.

Same afternoon, same street. On one porch, a family is setting out chairs for a party, balloons tied to the railing. Three doors down, the curtains are drawn, and cars are parked along the curb for a house of mourning. A man walks past both houses on the way to buy milk. Nobody on that street is doing life wrong. They're just in different hours of it. Kohelet has a poem for that street. It reads like a list, and it works like a clock.
screen: `A PARTY ON ONE PORCH.` → `MOURNING THREE DOORS DOWN.` → `DIFFERENT HOURS OF ONE LIFE.`

segments.voice: Ecclesiastes chapter three, in the words of the King James text: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven." Then the list begins. "A time to be born, and a time to die." A time to plant, and a time to pluck up. A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance. A time to keep silence, and a time to speak. And it ends: a time to love, and a time to hate; a time of war, and a time of peace. Notice how it's built. Pairs. Every line holds two opposites, side by side, and neither one cancels the other. The poem doesn't say mourning is bad and dancing is good. It says each has its hour. Yesterday, Kohelet called everything breath. Today he hints at something steadier underneath. A little further on in the chapter he says that God hath made every thing beautiful in his time. In its time. Not every moment is beautiful on its own. But each one has a place. Readers take the poem two ways. Some find comfort: grief won't last forever, and neither will this hard stretch. Others hear a challenge: you don't choose the season, but you can ask what this one is for. Is it a time to speak, or a time to keep silence? A time to plant, or a time to wait? The poem doesn't answer for you. It just insists the question is real. There is a time for everything.

segments.voice: First, a look back at this week. Mishlei and the first step through the door. A tree of life. Rakh. Each child's own way. Give him bread. Nothing stays in the hand. Now the practice: name the season you're in. Settle, and let a pair from the poem find you. A time to plant or to pluck up. To weep or to laugh. To keep silence or to speak. Don't choose the one you wish for; notice the one that's true. Say it quietly to yourself: this is a time to... and finish the line. If you pray, you can bring that season with you into prayer. The bell holds the time.
A season. Ecclesiastes three: to every thing there is a season, pairs of opposites, each with its own hour. Today's word.
Your line: a time for everything. Today, when you meet someone in a different season from yours, mourning or celebrating, let their hour be what it is. Day eight hundred fifty-four.
